outline.description: Introduce the problem of aligning large pre-trained language models (LMs) with human preferences. Explain why unsupervised pretraining yields powerful but not necessarily desirable behavior, and motivate learning from relative human preferences. Provide an overview of existing RLHF pipelines and their practical challenges, and summarize the main idea and contributions of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).
sections: Capabilities and misalignments of large language models
Why we need control and alignment: examples and desiderata
Human feedback modalities: demonstrations vs pairwise preferences
Overview of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF)
Practical challenges and costs of RLHF (sampling, instability, hyperparameter tuning)
High-level intuition behind DPO
Summary of paper contributions and roadmap of the textbook

outline.chapter_title: Essential Background: Language Models, Probabilities, and Optimization
outline.description: Cover the foundational concepts required to understand DPO: language models as conditional distributions, maximum likelihood training, log-probabilities, KL divergence, and basic optimization. This chapter ensures all readers share the same notation and intuitions.
sections: Language models as conditional distributions and policies
Sequence probabilities and token-level factorization
Maximum likelihood estimation and cross-entropy loss
Logits, softmax, and numerical stability
Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence: definition and properties
Regularization via KL penalties and the notion of a reference policy
Basic gradient-based optimization and stochastic gradient descent

outline.chapter_title: Reinforcement Learning, Policy Optimization, and Preference Learning
outline.description: Introduce the RL formulation relevant to language generation, RL objectives used in RLHF, policy gradient basics, actor-critic methods and PPO, and classical models for learning from pairwise preferences (Bradley–Terry, Plackett–Luce).
sections: Reinforcement learning for sequence generation: states, actions, rewards
Expected reward objectives and why sequences require special handling
Constrained RL objective: reward maximization with KL constraints
Policy gradient, REINFORCE, and variance reduction
Actor-critic algorithms and proximal policy optimization (PPO)
Bradley–Terry and Plackett–Luce models for pairwise and listwise preferences
From pairwise preference likelihoods to reward model training

outline.chapter_title: The Standard RLHF Pipeline: Detailed Walkthrough
outline.description: Present the canonical RLHF pipeline used in practice: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), preference collection and reward modeling, and RL policy fine-tuning. Discuss architectural choices, reward normalization, dataset construction, and failure modes commonly observed in practice.
sections: Phase 1 — Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): goals and procedures
Phase 2 — Sampling responses and collecting pairwise preferences
Phase 3 — Reward modeling: architectures, loss, and normalizing rewards
Phase 4 — Reinforcement learning: integrating learned rewards
Implementation details: initializing reward models from SFT, batching, and sampling
Common practical problems: reward overfitting, mode collapse, sampling costs
Existing heuristics: baselines, reward normalization, and ensembling

outline.description: Derive DPO step by step. Start from the KL-constrained RL objective, derive the closed-form optimal policy given a reward function, rearrange to express reward as a function of policy and reference policy, substitute into Bradley–Terry preference model, and obtain the DPO loss. Provide intuition for each mathematical step and discuss assumptions.
sections: Formal statement of the KL-constrained reward maximization objective
Deriving the optimal policy: exponentiating rewards and the partition function
Algebraic rearrangement: expressing reward in terms of policy and partition function
Cancellation of partition function when using pairwise preference models
Deriving the DPO maximum-likelihood policy objective
Intuition: what the DPO update is doing to log-probabilities
Extensions to Plackett–Luce and multi-answer preference models
Summary of assumptions and when the derivation applies

outline.chapter_title: Understanding and Interpreting the DPO Update
outline.description: Analyze the DPO gradient and dynamics. Explain the implicit reward represented by the policy, the adaptive weighting term in the gradient, and why this prevents degeneration compared to naive unlikelihood objectives. Relate DPO to classical statistical models (change-of-variables, identifiability).
sections: Computing the DPO gradient: detailed derivation
Implicit reward: r_hat = beta * log(pi_theta / pi_ref)
Role of the logistic-weighting term and why it stabilizes training
Comparison to naive unlikelihood and supervised preferences
Behavior on extreme examples and effect of beta
Interpreting DPO as MLE under a reparameterized Bradley–Terry model
Consequences for sample weighting and learning dynamics

outline.description: Present the theoretical properties of DPO: reward function equivalence classes, lemmas establishing invariances, theorem showing representation completeness of DPO parameterization, and analysis of instabilities in actor-critic methods. Provide proof sketches and intuition for each result.
sections: Equivalence classes of reward functions and additive prefix functions
Lemma: same preference distribution for rewards differing by prefix term
Lemma: same optimal policy for reward functions in same class
Theorem: representability — DPO's reparameterization spans reward classes
Proof sketch of the main theorem and key mathematical steps
Implications: identifiability and choice of canonical reward
Diagnosing actor-critic instabilities: the missing normalization term
Connections to control-as-inference and variance of policy gradients

outline.description: Turn theory into practice. Describe the end-to-end DPO algorithm, low-level implementation details for language models (computing sequence log-probabilities, handling long sequences, caching logits), strategies for constructing the reference policy, hyperparameter recommendations, and debugging tips.
sections: High-level DPO pipeline and pseudo-code
Constructing or obtaining the reference policy (pi_ref): SFT vs fitted reference
Computing sequence log-probabilities efficiently and numerically stably
Token-level vs sequence-level ratio computations and when to use each
Choice of beta: practical effects and tuning guidelines
Mini-batch composition and sampling from preference datasets
Training practicalities: learning rates, optimizers, and checkpointing
Monitoring training: metrics, detecting collapse, and early stopping

outline.chapter_title: Comparisons to Alternative Methods and Baselines
outline.description: Compare DPO to other approaches used in practice: PPO-based RLHF, Preferred-FT, Unlikelihood training, and Best-of-N selection. Provide conceptual and empirical trade-offs, when each method should be preferred, and how DPO avoids certain pitfalls.
sections: Preferred-FT (supervised on chosen completions): strengths and weaknesses
Unlikelihood training and naive likelihood ratio objectives
Best-of-N selection: decoupling reward modeling from policy optimization
PPO and actor-critic RLHF: complexity, instability, and hyperparameters
Computational cost comparisons and sampling overheads
When DPO outperforms and potential failure modes
Practical guidance for hybrid strategies (e.g., combining DPO with RL)

outline.description: Present the experimental setup and results from the paper: controlled sentiment generation, Reddit TL;DR summarization, and Anthropic single-turn dialogue. Describe datasets, evaluation methodology (including GPT-4 and human evaluations), baselines, experimental details, results and interpretation.
sections: Overview of experimental goals and evaluation criteria
Controlled sentiment generation: dataset, oracle reward, and reward-KL frontier
TL;DR summarization: dataset, SFT model, and GPT-4 evaluation
Single-turn dialogue (Anthropic HH): dataset, reference model training, and evaluation
Baselines evaluated (PPO, Preferred-FT, Unlikelihood, Best-of-N, prompting)
Quantitative results: reward-KL tradeoffs and win-rate plots
Out-of-distribution generalization experiment (CNN/DailyMail)
Human evaluation study and validating GPT-4 as an automatic judge
Empirical takeaways and analysis of failure cases

outline.description: Provide a concrete, step-by-step recipe for reproducing DPO experiments and training a DPO model on a new preference dataset. Include data preparation, SFT training, pi_ref construction, DPO training loop, evaluation setup, and a reproducibility checklist.
sections: Preparing and curating a pairwise preference dataset
Training or obtaining a supervised fine-tuned (SFT) model
Building the reference policy: options and recommended defaults
Implementing the DPO training loop (data loaders, losses, gradients)
Evaluation pipeline: automatic metrics, GPT-4 prompts, and human studies
Hyperparameter defaults and tuning plan
Logging, checkpointing, and experiment management
Reproducibility checklist and common pitfalls to avoid

outline.description: Explore extensions and variants of DPO, including multi-answer and listwise preferences, multi-turn dialogues, synthetic preference generation, integration with continual learning, and application to other modalities. Discuss research directions and open technical problems.
sections: Generalizing DPO to Plackett–Luce and listwise preferences
Adapting DPO to multi-turn dialogue and stateful policies
Using synthetic or AI-generated preference labels (RLAIF)
Hybrid methods: combining DPO with reward learning or RL
Applying DPO to other generative modalities (images, audio)
Continual preference learning and online updates
Open research questions: generalization, scaling, and robustness
Benchmarks and community resources to track progress

outline.description: Discuss the limitations of DPO, potential risks, ethical concerns, and responsible deployment practices. Cover reward hacking, dataset bias, evaluation sensitivity, and when human oversight and auditing are necessary.
sections: Limitations of the DPO theoretical framework and assumptions
Reward misspecification and reward hacking under implicit rewards
Dataset bias and representativeness of preference data
Evaluation sensitivity: effect of evaluator prompts and proxies (GPT-4)
Safety risks and adversarial preference manipulation
Transparency, auditing, and human-in-the-loop safeguards
Guidelines for responsible deployment and policy governance
Regulatory and societal implications

outline.description: Provide pedagogical exercises and project ideas to deepen understanding. Include derivation exercises, hands-on implementation tasks, experiments to reproduce and extend, and pointers to important related literature for further study.
sections: Mathematical exercises: deriving the optimal policy and DPO loss
Implementation project: DPO on a small LM with synthetic preferences
Empirical project: compare DPO, PPO, and Preferred-FT on a small dataset
Experimental project: study effect of beta and temperature on outputs
Theoretical project: explore identifiability and alternative reparameterizations
Advanced project: DPO with listwise preferences or multi-turn dialogues
Suggested reading: core RLHF and preference-learning papers
Datasets and code repositories to get started

outline.description: Recap the main insights of DPO, its practical and theoretical implications, and its potential to simplify preference-based alignment of language models. Conclude with a forward-looking perspective on integrating DPO into broader alignment systems and future research priorities.
sections: Recap of the DPO idea and why it matters
Key empirical and theoretical takeaways
When to use DPO in practice: decision criteria
Research challenges and promising directions
Final remarks on the role of preferences in aligning AI systems
Resources and next steps for students and practitioners
